fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Diet and the Lifestyle of Korean and Chinese Women: A Comparative Study Abstract Objective The study investigated and compared postpartum diet and behaviors, nutrition education, and psychological health status among Korean and Chinese postpartum women (0–6 months after delivery). Methods A total of 221 Korean mothers in Gyeonggi-do (South Korea) and 221 mothers in Jinhua (China) participated in the survey between November and December 2018, and the results were statistically analyzed using the SPSS Statistics 25.0 software. Results Many postpartum behaviors, such as postpartum diet pattern and care duration differed between Korean and Chinese mothers. The former showed a stronger desire for nutrition education compared with the latter (p < 0.001). Korean mothers' life and meal satisfaction, and contentment with their husband's support were all ~0.5 points higher compared with Chinese mothers, particularly regarding spousal support (p < 0.001). Postpartum depression stresses positively correlated with postpartum infant care stress and negatively correlated with life satisfaction. In addition, primipara mothers were more in need of infant care support and guidance concerning appropriate baby-feeding techniques compared with multipara mothers. Conclusion Traditional culture was a crucial factor that influenced the perceptions of postpartum women in South Korea and China. Culturally tailored nutrition education and exercise programs may benefit Korean and Chinese women after childbirth. Keywords: dietary behavior, health-related behavior, nutrition education, psychological health, postpartum Korean and Chinese women Introduction The postpartum period refers to the first 6 weeks after childbirth, also known as the fourth trimester. New mothers may experience a range of physiological and psychological issues after childbirth including hormonal changes, metabolism disorders, postpartum depression (PPD), childcare stress (CS), and anxiety. Although healthcare has significantly improved over the past decades, the data indicated that maternal mortality remains high (1). According to a World Health Organization report, approximately 11–17% of women died during childbirth, and 50–71% of maternity deaths occurred in the postpartum period (2). In addition to medical reasons, psychological health has become a topic of focus among Korean and Chinese researchers not only because it affects mortality during the postpartum period and the future health of mothers but also because how it manifests may vary according to culture. The most common and serious mental disorder during the postpartum period is PPD, a type of mood disorder that typically begins with childbirth and can predispose women to subsequent depression and other mental and physical health problems (3). Based on a review that collected and analyzed 40 relevant studies from 40 countries, the prevalence rate of PPD ranged from 0.5 to >60% (4). The exact cause of PPD is unclear but is likely related to a combination of physical and emotional factors. Studies have explored several possible individual factors associated with PPD including medication (5), maternal age, educational level, smoking history, hereditary factors, marriage status, family economic status, social support, and prenatal depression (6, 7). Conversely, postpartum anxiety and stress were a burden on mood and mental health, which correlated with harmful consequences for mothers, children, and families. A study found stress to be significantly linked to pre-pregnancy body mass index and PPD (8). The relationship between stress and mental health revealed that 30% of mothers reported experiencing psychological and physiological distress due to postpartum stress (9). Moreover, many studies found that the tendency to become anxious or depressed was greater in the presence of several risk factors, such as rapidly changing family structures, role-changing (10), and stressful life events during pregnancy (11), as well as parturition costs (12). To our knowledge, the factors affecting PPD and stress are complex, especially for the comparison of influencing factors in different countries. Since cultural custom plays an essential role in all human experiences and comprises several traditional beliefs, ideas, perspectives, cognitive styles, and dietary habits and behaviors, increasing attention has been drawn to the aspect of cultural background as it affects the postpartum period (13). For example, in South Korea and China, many new mothers believe that if postpartum care is inadequate, various symptoms of discomfort can arise and have a lifelong effect. Stress and PPD are culture-bound phenomena that are influenced by traditional beliefs (14). The traditional Chinese word zuo-yue-zi, as well as the Korean word Samchilil (which means “confinement period” or “doing the month”) (15), refers to an integrated set of customs that include beliefs and practices relevant during the postpartum period (16). In Asia, postpartum women have the custom of confinement, during which they have special diets, special behaviors, etc. Following childbirth, both the woman and her newborn need special postpartum care including help related to the acceptance of role-changing, postpartum activities, the maintenance of body hygiene, and food consumption. These steps are believed to restore maternal health and prevent future diseases. Many health problems, whether physiological or psychological, can be detected early through effective postpartum care that is based on cultural background (17). However, to our knowledge, no study has investigated and compared psychological health status and its relationship to postpartum traditional practices between Korean and Chinese cultures. fetched_contents.text: Safety of herbal medicine in the postpartum period: A hospital-based single-arm, prospective observational study (SAFEHERE-PC) Abstract Background Herbal medicines (HMs) are commonly used during the postpartum period in South Korea; however, comprehensive data regarding their safety remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the safety of HM use among postpartum women through the “SAFEty of HErbal medicine REgistry in Postpartum Care center” (SAFEHERE-PC) study. Methods A single-arm, prospective observational study was conducted from March to December 2024, enrolling 186 women within six weeks postpartum who were admitted to the postpartum care center of a Korean Medicine hospital. The study monitored adverse events (AEs) during HM use, collecting demographic information, medical history, herbal prescription details, and AE data. Reported AEs were analyzed using the WHO-UMC causality assessment and the Naranjo algorithm. Results Of the 186 participants, 4 (2.2 %) experienced AEs following HM administration, all of which were gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, loose stools). Three of the five events were managed with a short course of the herbal formula, and two cases resolved spontaneously without requiring medical intervention. Based on severity and clinical course, the events were classified as mild to moderate. Causality assessment using the WHO-UMC system classified four cases as "possible" and one as "certain", while the Naranjo scale indicated three cases as "possible" and two as "probable" in their association with HM use. Conclusion A low incidence of mild gastrointestinal AEs (2.2 % of patients; 0.6 % of prescriptions) was observed, with no serious AEs reported. These findings provide descriptive safety data specific to the formulations and clinical practices used at this hospital-based postpartum care center. Korean Medicine (KM) encompasses a range of therapeutic modalities, including herbal medicine (HM), acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping therapy, and physical therapy. These interventions are commonly used to manage various postpartum symptoms, including pain, systemic complaints, urogenital discomfort, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.8, 9 Among these, HM is particularly prevalent during pregnancy and postpartum recovery periods in many Asian countries. fetched_contents.text: Pregnancy, prescription medicines and the potential risk of herb-drug interactions: a cross-sectional survey Abstract Background Pregnant women are routinely prescribed medicines while self-medicating with herbal natural products to treat predominantly pregnancy related conditions. The aim of this study was to assess the potential for herb-drug interactions (HDIs) in pregnant women and to explore possible herb-drug interactions and their potential clinical significance. Methods A cross-sectional survey of women during early pregnancy or immediately postpartum in North-East Scotland. Outcome measures included; Prescription medicines use excluding vitamins and potential HDIs assessed using Natural Medicines Comprehensive Database. Results The survey was completed by 889 respondents (73% response rate). 45.3% (403) reported the use of at least one prescription medicine, excluding vitamins. Of those taking prescription medicines, 44.9% (181) also reported concurrent use of at least one HNP (Range 1–12). A total of 91 different prescription medicines were reported by respondents using HNPs. Of those taking prescription medicines, 44.9% (181) also reported concurrent use of at least one HNP (Range 1–12). Thirty-four herb-drug interactions were identified in 23 (12.7%) women with the potential to increase the risk of postpartum haemorrhage, alter maternal haemodynamics, and enhance maternal/fetal CNS depression. Almost all were rated as moderate (93.9%), one as a potentially major (ginger and nifedipine) and only one minor (ondansetron and chamomile). Conclusion Almost half of pregnant women in this study were prescribed medicines excluding vitamins and minerals and almost half of these used HNPs. Potential moderate to severe HDIs were identified in an eighth of the study cohort. Healthcare professionals should be aware that the concurrent use of HNPs and prescription medicines during pregnancy is common and carries potential risks. Mini-report on the traditional postpartum soup landscape

Across East Asia, postpartum herbal soups are a widespread cultural practice, with several recipes and ingredients commonly recommended by older relatives. The most commonly mentioned soups include Korean seaweed soup, Chinese fish and papaya soup, black chicken herbal soup, pork rib and lotus root soup, and postpartum herbal mixtures such as the one described as “Ah-ma’s Postpartum Herbal Soup” [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In the Chinese context, these soups are often framed around the postpartum “confinement” period, during which the body is believed to need special care and nourishment [N2-F4]. 

The ingredients most often highlighted are papaya, skin-on peanuts, ginger, pig feet or pork trotters, goji berries, and seaweed, with additional ingredients such as lotus root and black chicken appearing in specific recipes [N2-R3][N2-R1]. The traditional benefits claimed for these soups are broadly centered on healing, lactation support, wound healing, and restoring strength after childbirth [N2-R2][N2-R3]. For example, seaweed soup is said to be high in iron and micronutrients and to help with healing after birth [N2-R1], while fish and papaya soup is linked to milk production [N1-R4]. Black chicken herbal soup is associated with building blood, and pork rib and lotus root soup with aiding digestion [N1-R4]. Goji berries and red dates are also often included for their claimed antioxidant, energy, and nutrient-support roles [N5-R4].

Cultural and generational beliefs strongly shape the use of these soups. In both Korea and China, the postpartum period is tied to a set of customs, including special diets and behaviors, that are believed to restore maternal health and prevent future diseases [N2-F4]. The Korean “Samchilil” (“confinement period”) and the Chinese “zuo-yue-zi” reflect an integrated cultural system in which postpartum care is not just medical but also ritualized and generational [N2-F4]. Older relatives often insist on these soups because they are seen as part of a traditional recovery framework, and their use can be reinforced by the idea that inadequate postpartum care may lead to long-term health problems [N2-F4]. This means the practice is less about isolated recipes and more about a shared belief in the power of warmth, nourishment, and tradition to support recovery [N2-R1][N2-R3].

Overall, the traditional landscape shows that East Asian postpartum soups are highly localized and recipe-specific, but they share common ingredients and a common narrative: these soups are meant to heal, support lactation, and restore strength, and they are passed down through generations as part of postpartum cultural care [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R3][N2-F4].

Mini-report on modern medical safety and evidence

Modern medical evidence suggests that postpartum herbal soups are not universally safe and that many ingredients carry known risks, especially when used with drugs or in combination with other herbs. The safest conclusion is that the ingredients are **not generally safe in a blanket sense**; instead, their safety depends on the specific herb, dosage, concurrent medications, and individual health status [N3-R1][N3-R4][N4-F3]. A hospital-based study of herbal medicine use in the postpartum period found a low incidence of mild gastrointestinal adverse events, but no serious AEs, and it emphasized that safety data remain limited [N3-F2]. This finding is useful, but it also highlights the gap between real-world use and rigorous safety evidence [N3-F2].

Evidence for nutrient support is mixed. Some traditional ingredients are plausible for nourishment and digestion, such as seaweed for iron and micronutrients [N2-R1], and black chicken for blood-building [N1-R4]. However, the evidence provided in the search results does not show strong modern proof that these soups consistently improve postpartum nutrition or recovery beyond what could be achieved through balanced, modern diets [N1-R4][N2-R1]. The key limitation here is that traditional soups are often bundled with multiple herbs and ingredients, making it hard to isolate the effects of any single component [N3-F2][N5-F1].

Evidence for infection risk is limited in the provided materials, but the broader safety literature suggests that herbal products can introduce risks through contamination, adulteration, or interaction with medical treatments [N4-F3]. The herb-drug interaction literature notes that concurrent use of herbs and prescription medicines is common and can produce moderate to severe interactions, including increased postpartum hemorrhage risk, altered maternal hemodynamics, and enhanced CNS depression [N4-F3]. This is especially relevant because postpartum women may be on medications for pain, blood pressure, or other conditions, and herbs can change how those medications work [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that many in vitro interactions have not been proven in human trials, so claims about safety or efficacy cannot be assumed from traditional use alone [N4-R2].

Evidence for drug interactions is stronger and more worrisome. The postpartum herbal medicine study found a low incidence of mild AEs, but it also notes that adverse events were not fully understood and that causality assessment varied [N3-F2]. The herb-drug interaction review found 34 potential interactions in 23 women, including interactions that could increase postpartum hemorrhage risk and enhance CNS depression [N4-F3]. Specific herbs and ingredients in postpartum soups may matter here: for example, Dong Quai is explicitly noted as increasing bleeding risk in patients on warfarin or antiplatelet drugs and as best avoided during breastfeeding [N5-F1]. Goji berries and red dates are not shown to have major drug interaction evidence in the provided sources, but the broader point remains that any herb used with medications should be treated with caution [N5-R4][N5-F1].

Limitations of traditional versus modern evidence are clear. Traditional evidence is largely based on cultural practice, anecdote, and long-standing recipe use, which can suggest a role for an herb but does not prove safety or efficacy [N2-F4][N5-F1]. Modern evidence is more rigorous, but it is still limited in scope and often comes from observational or registry studies rather than large randomized controlled trials [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The provided sources also show that safety assessments are incomplete and that many herb-drug interactions remain poorly understood [N4-F3][N5-F1]. As a result, it is reasonable to say that traditional beliefs are often based on generations of use and cultural narrative, but they should not be treated as proof of safety in a modern medical sense [N2-F4][N3-F2][N4-F3].

In short: the ingredients are not automatically safe, they can have nutrient-support plausibility, they may interact with drugs, and modern evidence is limited and mostly descriptive rather than conclusive [N3-F2][N4-F3][N5-F1].

When to use these soups and when to avoid them  
Traditional postpartum soups are often recommended for short-term recovery support after childbirth, especially during the first weeks when the body is healing and lactation is being established [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F4]. However, the evidence suggests that many ingredients carry risks and that safety is not guaranteed simply because they are traditional [N3-F2][N4-F3]. New mothers should use these soups cautiously, especially if they are taking medications, are on blood thinners, have a history of bleeding disorders, or are breastfeeding [N3-F2][N5-F1].  

The safest approach is to use these soups only after consulting a doctor and to avoid them if the mother has a known allergy, is on medications that may interact with herbs, or has a condition that makes bleeding more likely [N3-F2][N5-F1]. Some ingredients, such as Dong Quai, are explicitly noted as increasing bleeding risk and best avoided during breastfeeding [N5-F1]. Seaweed-based soups may also carry nutrient-related concerns and should not be treated as a substitute for balanced postpartum nutrition [N2-R1][N4-F3]. In general, these soups are better suited as occasional supportive foods rather than as routine or mandatory postpartum staples [N1-R4][N3-F2].

How to balance tradition with modern medical guidance  
Older relatives’ insistence on these soups often reflects cultural tradition and generational care beliefs, which can be meaningful and comforting [N2-F4]. But modern medical guidance should not be ignored. The evidence supports the idea that traditional soups may have some plausible nutritional roles, such as iron, micronutrient, or digestive support, but it does not prove that they are safe or effective for every woman [N1-R4][N2-R1][N3-F2].  

The best balance is to respect tradition while seeking evidence-based assessment. If a relative recommends a soup, a mother should ask whether it contains any herbs with known risks and whether it is compatible with any medications she is taking [N3-F2][N5-F1]. She should also ask whether the recipe is necessary for recovery or whether simpler, safer foods could provide similar benefits [N3-F2][N4-F3]. In other words, tradition can guide choice, but modern medical advice should determine whether a soup is appropriate for her specific situation [N2-F4][N3-F2].

What questions a mother should ask her doctor  
A mother should ask her doctor the following questions:  
1. Is this soup or recipe safe for me, especially if I am on medications or have a medical condition? [N3-F2][N5-F1]  
2. Are any herbs in the soup likely to interact with my current medications, including blood thinners or other drugs? [N4-F3][N5-F1]  
3. Could this soup increase the risk of bleeding or other complications? [N3-F2][N5-F1]  
4. Is there a safer alternative that can support recovery or lactation without the risks? [N1-R4][N3-F2]  
5. Should I avoid this soup if I am breastfeeding? [N5-F1]  
6. Do I need to stop or limit this soup if I develop symptoms such as gastrointestinal discomfort, bleeding, or allergic reactions? [N3-F2][N5-F1]  

In short, traditional postpartum soups can be part of a cultural care framework, but they are not automatically safe or universally beneficial [N2-F4][N3-F2]. New mothers should use them with caution, ask questions, and rely on modern medical guidance to make informed decisions [N3-F2][N4-F3][N5-F1].
